---
title: "Git basics"
---

A general introduction to Git: what it does, the everyday commands, and
how to work with GitHub. For the commands specific to the `gflownet`
library (checking out PRs, notes branches, comparing PR branches), see
[Git for the gflownet library](git.qmd).

## What Git is

Git is a **version control system**: it records snapshots of a project
over time, so you can see what changed, go back to an earlier version,
and work on several versions in parallel.

- A **repository** (repo) is a project tracked by Git. Its whole history
  lives in a hidden `.git` folder at the root of the project.
- A **commit** is a snapshot of the project, with a message, an author,
  a date and a unique id (a hash such as `3e8e13c`).
- A **branch** is a movable name pointing to a commit. Each new commit on
  the branch moves it forward.
- **Git** runs on your computer. **GitHub** is a website that hosts
  repositories, so that you can back them up and share them.

## The three areas

| Area | What it is | Moved there with |
|---|---|---|
| **Working directory** | your files, as you edit them | (just edit) |
| **Staging area** | the changes selected for the next commit | `git add` |
| **Repository** | the saved history of commits | `git commit` |

Working with a remote (GitHub) adds a fourth place, reached with
`git push` (see [Remotes](#remotes-working-with-github)).

You choose what goes into each commit: editing three files and staging
only two gives a commit with those two files, and the third stays as an
unstaged change.

## Setting up Git

Once per computer:

```bash
git --version                                # check that Git is installed
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main  # name new repos' first branch main
git config --list                            # see your settings
```

The name and email are written into every commit you make. To keep your
real email private on GitHub, use the `@users.noreply.github.com`
address from your GitHub email settings.

## Starting a repository

```bash
# Turn an existing folder into a repository
cd my-project
git init

# Or copy an existing repository (with its whole history)
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git my-folder   # choose the folder name
```

## The everyday cycle

```bash
git status                 # what changed? what is staged?
git diff                   # unstaged changes, line by line
git add file.py            # stage one file
git add .                  # stage everything in the current folder
git diff --staged          # what will go into the commit
git commit -m "Add data loader"
git log --oneline          # the history, one line per commit
```

Good commit messages say **what** the commit does, in the imperative:
"Fix off-by-one in mask", not "fixed stuff". Small commits that each do
one thing are easier to understand and to undo.

### `.gitignore`

A `.gitignore` file at the root lists files that Git should never track:
data, outputs, secrets, environment folders.

```text
# .gitignore
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
data/
logs/
.env
```

It only affects untracked files. To stop tracking a file that is already
committed, while keeping it on disk: `git rm --cached file`.

::: {.callout-warning}
Never commit passwords, API keys or tokens. Deleting them in a later
commit is not enough: they stay in the history. If it happens, revoke
the key.
:::

## Looking at the history

```bash
git log                        # full history
git log --oneline --graph --all   # compact, with branches drawn
git log -- path/to/file.py     # commits that touched a file
git show 3e8e13c               # what a commit changed
git diff main feature          # differences between two branches
git blame file.py              # who last changed each line, and when
```

## Undoing things

| Situation | Command |
|---|---|
| discard your edits to a file (not staged) | `git restore file.py` |
| unstage a file (keep the edits) | `git restore --staged file.py` |
| fix the message or content of the **last** commit (not pushed yet) | `git commit --amend` |
| undo the last commit, keep its changes | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` |
| create a new commit that reverses an old one | `git revert <hash>` |
| delete untracked files | `git clean -n` (preview), then `git clean -f` |

`HEAD` means "the commit you are on", and `HEAD~1` is the one before.

::: {.callout-warning}
`git restore`, `git reset --hard` and `git clean -f` delete uncommitted
work for good. On commits that are already pushed, prefer `git revert`,
which adds a new commit instead of rewriting the history others have.
:::

If you lose a commit (after a bad reset or rebase), `git reflog` lists
every position `HEAD` has been at, and you can get back with
`git switch -c rescue <hash>`.

## Branches

Branches let you work on something without touching `main`: a feature,
an experiment, a fix.

```bash
git branch                  # list branches (* = current)
git switch -c new-feature   # create a branch and switch to it
git switch main             # switch to an existing branch
git switch -                # go back to the previous branch
git branch -d new-feature   # delete a merged branch
git branch -D new-feature   # delete it even if not merged
```

`git switch` changes the files in your folder to match the branch. Commit
or stash your changes first (see [Stash](#stash-putting-changes-aside)).
Older tutorials use `git checkout` for the same thing.

### Merging

To bring the commits of `new-feature` into `main`:

```bash
git switch main
git merge new-feature
```

If both branches changed the same lines, Git stops with a **conflict**
and marks the file:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
threshold = 0.5
=======
threshold = 0.7
>>>>>>> new-feature
```

Edit the file to keep the right version, delete the markers, then:

```bash
git add file.py
git commit                 # completes the merge
# or give up and go back to before the merge:
git merge --abort
```

### Rebasing

`git rebase main` (run on `new-feature`) replays the commits of
`new-feature` on top of the latest `main`. The result has the same
content as a merge, but a straight history without a merge commit.

- Conflicts are resolved the same way, then `git rebase --continue`
  (or `git rebase --abort`).
- Rebase rewrites commits. Only rebase branches that nobody else has
  pulled.

## Stash: putting changes aside

```bash
git stash          # save uncommitted changes and clean the folder
git stash list     # see the stashes
git stash pop      # bring the last stash back
git stash drop     # delete the last stash
```

Useful when you need to switch branches but aren't ready to commit.

## Remotes: working with GitHub

A **remote** is a copy of the repository somewhere else. The one you
cloned from is called `origin`.

```bash
git remote -v                         # list remotes
git remote add origin git@github.com:user/repo.git   # connect a local repo

git fetch origin                      # download new commits, change nothing
git pull                              # fetch + merge into the current branch
git push                              # upload your commits
git push -u origin new-feature        # first push of a new branch
                                      # (-u remembers where to push next time)
git branch -vv                        # local branches and how far
                                      # ahead/behind their remote they are
```

- `fetch` is always safe: it only downloads. `pull` also changes your
  current branch.
- `push` is refused if the remote has commits you don't have. Pull
  first, fix any conflicts, then push again.
- **SSH vs HTTPS URLs.** `git@github.com:...` uses an SSH key, and
  `https://github.com/...` uses a token. Pick one and set it up once in
  your GitHub settings.

### Pull requests and forks

A **pull request** (PR) is a GitHub feature, not a Git one: it asks for
a branch to be merged into another, with a review.

1. Create a branch, commit, and `git push -u origin my-branch`.
2. On GitHub, open a PR from `my-branch` into `main`.
3. Push more commits to the same branch to update the PR.
4. Once it is merged, update your `main` with `git switch main` and
   `git pull`, then delete the branch.

If you can't push to a repository, **fork** it on GitHub (your own copy),
clone your fork, push to it, and open the PR from the fork.

## Tags

A tag is a fixed name for a commit, typically a release or the code
behind a paper's results:

```bash
git tag v1.0
git tag -a paper-v1 -m "Code for the submission"
git push origin --tags
```

## Typical workflow

```bash
git switch main
git pull                         # start from the latest main
git switch -c fix-mask           # one branch per task
# ... edit ...
git status
git add gflownet/envs/tree/tree.py
git commit -m "Fix backward mask of the tree env"
git push -u origin fix-mask      # then open a PR on GitHub
```

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| set your identity | `git config --global user.name / user.email` |
| new repo / copy a repo | `git init` / `git clone <url>` |
| what changed? | `git status`, `git diff`, `git diff --staged` |
| stage / commit | `git add <file>`, `git commit -m "..."` |
| history | `git log --oneline --graph --all` |
| discard edits / unstage | `git restore <file>`, `git restore --staged <file>` |
| fix the last commit | `git commit --amend` |
| reverse a pushed commit | `git revert <hash>` |
| find a lost commit | `git reflog` |
| new branch / switch | `git switch -c <name>` / `git switch <name>` |
| merge a branch into the current one | `git merge <branch>` |
| replay commits onto main | `git rebase main` |
| put changes aside | `git stash`, `git stash pop` |
| download / update / upload | `git fetch`, `git pull`, `git push` |
| first push of a branch | `git push -u origin <branch>` |
| ignore files | `.gitignore` |
